mcqs.question: In a layered frontend architecture, what actually makes the separation meaningful?
options: The dependency direction: stable business rules must not import volatile UI or transport details.
The folder names: code must live in folders named presentation, application, domain, and infrastructure.
The layer count: every serious app needs exactly four layers, and a small app is just an unfinished one.
The technology mix: each layer must use a different framework or library to prove independence.
mcqs.explanation: The rule is separation by responsibility, not by file extension: the names matter less than dependency direction, and a small app may not need four layers while a large app benefits when the separation reduces coupling and eases tests and migrations. The strongest distractor (folder names) fails because renaming folders changes nothing about the import graph: a component can still import an HTTP client directly, so the structure is cosmetic without an enforced dependency rule.

mcqs.question: A team organizes the frontend by features. Which practice actually preserves the benefit of that organization?
options: A global components/, hooks/, and utils/ tree kept alongside the features, so shared code has one home.
A small public API per feature plus enforced import rules, so no feature reaches into another feature's internals.
Free cross-folder imports between features, since everything lives in the same repository anyway.
Forcing every helper, however tiny, into a feature folder so that nothing is ever shared.
mcqs.explanation: Feature organization works when each feature exposes a small public API and import rules prevent reaching into another feature's internals, with genuinely shared code in an explicit shared area. The strongest distractor (the global tree) fails because it recreates the exact coupling feature organization exists to avoid: unrelated code becomes coupled in components, hooks, and utils folders, and ownership and deletion get harder. The last distractor overcorrects: stable primitives and cross-cutting infrastructure can remain shared.

mcqs.question: A user flow works in Vite's dev server. What does that prove about production?
options: It proves production works, because the dev server and the production build run the same module pipeline.
Nothing by itself: development is native-ESM-oriented serving while production is a separate bundling flow, so the built artifact must be validated on representative flows.
It proves production works as long as the dev server was started in production mode.
It proves nothing, because Vite has no production build and webpack must be added for deployment.
mcqs.explanation: Vite provides a dev server and a distinct production build flow with configurable targets, entries, and code splitting (https://vite.dev/guide/build), so a dev-server success only exercises the dev pipeline. The strongest distractor (same pipeline) fails because development and production are different flows in Vite; the last distractor fails in the opposite direction, since Vite does ship a production build, and the mode distractor fails because mode selection changes which env files load, not which pipeline serves the code.

mcqs.question: Why should a workspace package expose deliberate entry points through package.json exports?
options: So every internal file becomes importable from outside, giving consumers maximum flexibility.
Because a barrel file that re-exports everything is the recommended default entry point.
So consumers depend on supported names and contracts rather than the directory layout, letting internal refactors stay internal.
Because exports only matter for packages published to a registry, not for internal workspace packages.
mcqs.explanation: A public entry point is a boundary you can evolve deliberately: consumers depend on supported names and contracts, and the exports field can enumerate entry points while avoiding exposing implementation files (https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html#exports). The strongest distractor (the barrel default) fails because Turborepo's guidance notes barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). The last distractor fails because boundaries matter inside the workspace too: deep imports turn internal refactors into repository-wide edits.

mcqs.question: A pnpm workspace package declares @acme/ui as workspace:*, but no local package matches at install time. What happens?
options: pnpm silently installs the best-matching @acme/ui from the registry so the build keeps moving.
pnpm creates a placeholder stub and prints a warning to address later.
pnpm rewrites the dependency to a plain semver range and retries the registry automatically.
Installation fails, because workspace: resolves only to a matching local workspace package.
mcqs.explanation: The workspace: protocol tells pnpm to resolve only to a matching local workspace package; if the requested local version is absent, installation fails, which exposes accidental version drift early and keeps local development and CI deterministic (https://pnpm.io/workspaces). The strongest distractor (silent registry fallback) describes exactly the failure mode the protocol was designed to prevent, and it is what would happen with a plain version spec.

mcqs.question: A Turborepo build task sets inputs to ["src/**"], but the build also reads vite.config.ts and the DEPLOY_ENV variable. What is the risk?
options: Cache hits can restore stale artifacts, because output-affecting inputs are missing from the hash.
No risk: Turborepo automatically discovers every config file and environment variable a task reads.
The task fails immediately with a missing-cache-input error, so the mistake is self-detecting.
Only the dev server is affected; production builds bypass the task cache entirely.
mcqs.explanation: A cache is only safe when all output-affecting inputs, including relevant environment values and configuration, are represented in the hash; Turborepo hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results and assumes tasks are deterministic (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching). Specifying inputs also opts out of the default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). The strongest distractor (auto-discovery) fails because Turborepo hashes exactly what is declared: an undeclared env var is invisible to the fingerprint and nothing errors.

mcqs.question: In Nx, app A depends on lib L (a project-graph edge). What does that imply when running tests?
options: A's test automatically waits for L's test, because every project edge implies the same-named target dependency.
L's test waits for A's test, since dependents are validated before their dependencies.
Nothing automatic: A's test does not wait for L's test unless a task dependency such as ^test is configured.
Nx refuses to run both tests in one invocation and requires two separate commands.
mcqs.explanation: The project graph describes projects and their source or dependency relationships, while the task graph describes concrete targets and the task-to-task dependencies needed for one invocation; two projects can depend on a library while their test tasks run independently unless a ^test relationship is configured (https://nx.dev/concepts/mental-model). The strongest distractor fails because it mirrors the project graph onto the task graph, serializing work that has no ordering requirement and conflating architecture with scheduling.

mcqs.question: A Vite app gates verbose logging with: if (import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG). The env file sets VITE_DEBUG=false in production. What happens?
options: Verbose logging turns on: the value is the string "false", which is truthy.
The gate works, because Vite coerces "false" to boolean false at build time.
The build fails with a type error for using a string where a boolean is expected.
The variable is undefined in production, because VITE_ variables are only defined in development.
mcqs.explanation: Vite exposes VITE_-prefixed variables through import.meta.env as strings, so they must be parsed into booleans, numbers, and URLs at a typed configuration boundary (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (automatic coercion) fails because no coercion happens; the same root cause breaks strict comparisons too, since 'true' === true is false. The last distractor misreads modes: files like .env.production exist precisely to define values for production builds.

mcqs.question: When is a micro-frontend architecture justified?
options: Whenever the codebase passes a size threshold, because large apps cannot be built any other way.
Whenever more than one team touches the frontend, since multiple teams require separate deployables.
Whenever teams want different frameworks, because framework freedom is the primary benefit.
When independent delivery and team autonomy solve a real organizational or migration problem, not merely because the application is large.
mcqs.explanation: Micro-frontends pay off when independent delivery and team autonomy solve a real organizational or migration problem; the browser is still one runtime where DOM ownership, navigation, authentication, observability, failure handling, and shared dependencies need explicit rules (https://single-spa.js.org/docs/microfrontends-concept/). The strongest distractor (team count) fails because multiple teams can ship independently inside one deployable; the framework-freedom distractor fails because multiple frameworks mainly make sense during migration and increase runtime and operational cost.

mcqs.question: Host and remote both declare React in Module Federation's shared config. Why might the page still end up with two React copies?
options: Share scopes choose a copy based on version requirements and singleton settings; incompatible ranges or a missing singleton policy can load multiple copies.
Federation always dedupes shared dependencies automatically, so two copies are impossible.
React cannot be listed in shared at all; each build must bundle it privately.
Duplicate output.uniqueName values always duplicate every shared dependency.
mcqs.explanation: Shared dependencies are registered in a share scope rather than necessarily bundled privately, and version requirements and singleton settings influence which shared copy is consumed, so stateful libraries like React need an intentional compatibility policy (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). The strongest distractor (automatic dedupe) fails because sharing is negotiated at runtime, not guaranteed. The uniqueName distractor confuses two documented failure modes: duplicate output.uniqueName values collide on the runtime name, they do not control share-scope version selection.

mcqs.question: One frontend artifact must be promoted unchanged through dev, staging, and production with different API URLs. What is the sound design?
options: Build a separate artifact per environment using .env.staging and .env.production, which keeps each build simple.
Keep everything in import.meta.env and treat it as a runtime configuration service the app reads after deploy.
Typed, validated build-time public values plus environment-specific non-secret values injected at deployment or request time and schema-validated before bootstrap.
Encrypt the secrets into the bundle and decrypt them in the browser at runtime, so only the app can read them.
mcqs.explanation: Build-time values are immutable once bundled, so a single promoted artifact needs non-secret runtime configuration injected from a controlled server response, HTML bootstrap, or equivalent deployment mechanism, with its schema validated before bootstrapping (https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode). The strongest distractor (per-environment builds) fails because mode-specific env files are selected at build time, producing different artifacts, which is exactly what promotion forbids. The encryption distractor fails because a browser can inspect every value it receives; encryption the client can undo is not secrecy.

scenarios.prompt: This Vite app cannot turn debug logging off in production, and a security review flagged the config module. Find every defect and rewrite the configuration boundary.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Walkthrough: (1) The debug gate is broken because env values are strings: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG is the string 'false', which is truthy, so verbose logging is enabled in production. The same root cause would break a === true check, since 'true' === true is false. (2) The payments secret is a leak: Vite bundles VITE_-prefixed variables into client code at build time, so anything prefixed VITE_ is public configuration and must never contain secrets. The charge call must go through a backend or serverless function that holds the secret server-side; the client only sends the card token to our own endpoint. (3) apiUrl is an unparsed string: parse it with new URL(...) at the boundary so a malformed value fails at startup or build time, not at the first fetch. (4) Nothing is validated: required public values should be validated at startup or build time so a missing VITE_API_URL fails loudly instead of producing undefined URLs. Rewrite: a single config module that reads import.meta.env once, parses and validates, and exports a typed object; the rest of the app imports typed config, never import.meta.env. Sketch: const raw = { apiUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, debug: import.meta.env.VITE_DEBUG }; if (!raw.apiUrl) throw new Error('VITE_API_URL is required'); export const config = { apiUrl: new URL(raw.apiUrl), debug: raw.debug === 'true' };. Operationally, remember that shell variables have higher priority than .env files and that the dev server must be restarted after changing env files.
rubric: Identifies the string-truthiness bug: 'false' is a truthy string, so debug logging is on in production, and no automatic coercion exists.
Identifies the secret leak: VITE_ values are bundled into the client at build time, so the payments secret must move to a backend or serverless function.
Parses and validates at one typed boundary: URL construction, boolean parsing, and required-value checks instead of scattering raw strings.
States the operational facts: values are strings, shell variables override .env files, and the dev server needs a restart after env changes.
Keeps the fix at a single seam so application code imports a typed config module rather than import.meta.env directly.

scenarios.prompt: CI builds this monorepo. A pull request that only touched apps/web/src/** got a cache hit for the apps/web build task, and the staging deployment shipped production API URLs. The apps/web build script is `vite build`; its vite.config.ts reads process.env.DEPLOY_ENV to bake the API base URL into the bundle, and CI sets DEPLOY_ENV=staging on the staging pipeline. Diagnose the caching failure and fix the task definition.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: the cache is not broken, the cache model is. inputs defines what contributes to the task's hash, and the build's output depends on two things the hash never sees: apps/web/vite.config.ts (task configuration) and the DEPLOY_ENV environment variable. The PR changed only src files, so its hash matched the previously cached production build and Turborepo restored that artifact: a correct hit against an incomplete fingerprint. Note also that specifying inputs opts out of Turborepo's default behavior of hashing all source-controlled files in the package, so this narrowing is what removed vite.config.ts from the hash in the first place (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks). Fix: include the config file in inputs, for example ["src/**", "vite.config.ts"], or restore default behavior with ["$TURBO_DEFAULT$", "!README.md"]-style exclusions of files proven irrelevant; and declare DEPLOY_ENV as an environment cache input (the task-level env key, or globalEnv / globalDependencies when the value affects many tasks) so a changed value misses cache (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/caching). Keep outputs: ["dist/**"] so hits still restore the bundle. Verification: use --dry or --summarize to inspect what is actually hashed, and compare against a clean build when debugging a suspected stale hit. The governing principle: Turborepo assumes tasks are deterministic and hashes inputs to decide whether to restore results, so a cache hit is never evidence of correctness; narrow inputs only with proof that omitted files cannot affect the output.
rubric: Explains that a cache hit only proves the hashed inputs matched, and that the omitted config file and env var made the fingerprint incomplete rather than the cache broken.
Knows that specifying inputs replaces the default all-source-controlled-files behavior, which is how vite.config.ts fell out of the hash.
Fixes the task definition: config files added to inputs, DEPLOY_ENV declared as an environment cache input (env, or globalEnv/globalDependencies where appropriate), outputs kept.
Recommends verification tooling: dry runs or run summaries, and comparing against a clean build before trusting narrowed inputs.
Applies the determinism assumption and rejects 'cache hit equals correctness' reasoning when explaining the incident.

scenarios.prompt: Refactor this workspace UI package so consumers can only use a deliberate public API. Explain what breaks, why it breaks, and why the change is worth it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Problems: (1) The barrel re-exports everything, including the internal merge-styles helper, so every internal name is de facto public API; Turborepo's repository guidance notes that barrel files can be difficult for compilers and bundlers and recommends explicit exports (https://turbo.build/repo/docs/crafting-your-repository/structuring-a-repository). (2) apps/marketing deep-imports @acme/ui/dist/internal/button, which works only because the path is currently reachable; it is not a contract, and a reorganization of the package's output would break it with no version bump or deprecation signal. (3) package.json uses main with no exports field, so nothing enumerates what consumers may use. Refactor: add an exports map that enumerates deliberate entry points, for example { ".": "./dist/index.js" } plus granular entries like "./button" only if consumers genuinely need them; keep the barrel small and explicit, exporting only public names and nothing from internal/; remove merge-styles from the public surface (inline it, or split it into its own package if it is genuinely shared); migrate the deep import in apps/marketing to the public entry as part of the same change; and test the public surface as an API so accidental exports fail CI. Payoff: internal refactors stop being repository-wide edits, ownership and API review become clear, dependency analysis works, and compilers and bundlers avoid barrel overhead. The package contract matters more than the source folder layout.
rubric: Adds a package.json exports map that enumerates entry points and stops exposing implementation files.
Removes internal exports from the barrel and keeps the public surface narrow, citing the compiler and bundler cost of giant barrels.
Migrates the existing deep import to the public entry instead of leaving a silently broken consumer.
Treats the public surface as a tested contract with documented compatibility expectations.
Justifies the change in terms of refactoring safety, ownership, and dependency analysis, not just tidiness.

scenarios.prompt: This shell mounts two federated remotes. Each remote works alone in its own dev server, but mounted together one remote's React hooks throw and the console shows a shared-scope version warning. Diagnose every defect against Module Federation's documented mechanics, then list the organizational policies that are missing.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Defects: (1) The shell statically imports both remotes at the top of its entry. A remote module is asynchronous: loading the container and evaluating the exposed module are separate steps, and the host must initialize a share scope, pass it to the container's init, and obtain modules through get (https://webpack.js.org/concepts/module-federation/). A synchronous import assumes that handshake has already happened, which is not guaranteed at module-evaluation time; the shell needs an async boundary before rendering remote content. (2) remote_two's config was copy-pasted and still declares name: 'remote_one'. Every build needs a unique runtime name to avoid collisions; duplicate output.uniqueName values are a documented failure mode, and two containers claiming the same runtime name can collide when mounted together. (3) The shared React policy is inconsistent: remote_one requires ^18.2.0 with singleton, remote_two requires ^18.0.0 without singleton. Share scopes choose which copy is consumed based on version requirements and singleton settings, so without a shared, intentional compatibility policy for a stateful library like React, the runtime can load two React copies and hook state breaks, which matches the hook errors and the shared-scope warning. Policies to define before more remotes ship: treat remotes as runtime dependencies of the shell, not imports with URLs; pin or select remote versions deliberately with versioned remote URLs; define behavior when a manifest or entry cannot load and when an exposed contract is missing; keep a known-good fallback where the product requires continuity; make loading, initialization, and rendering failures observable by remote and version; assign ownership for shared libraries; and run compatibility tests for exposed APIs in each remote's pipeline, with release, rollback, security review, and incident-response processes built on those mechanics.
rubric: Identifies the async violation: remotes load through container init and get, so a static import at entry evaluation is wrong and the shell needs an async boundary.
Identifies the duplicate name/uniqueName collision from the copy-pasted config as a documented failure mode.
Explains share-scope version selection and why consistent requiredVersion plus singleton matters for stateful libraries like React.
Proposes organizational policy: versioned remote URLs with deliberate pinning, fallback behavior, and failure observability by remote and version.
Frames remotes as runtime dependencies of the shell, including compatibility tests for exposed APIs and shared-library ownership.
